chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn Ali from Abd al-Samad ibn Bashir from Atiyyah, brother of Abu al-Comm, said:
I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'The companions of al-Mughira forbid me from eating al-qadeed (dried meat) that fire has not touched.' He said, 'There is no harm in eating it.'

key_terms.أَصْحَابَ الْمُغِيرَةِ: The companions of al-Mughira, a group of early jurists whose opinions are often cited in contrast or comparison.
key_terms.الْقَدِيدِ: Dried meat, specifically meat that has been dried without the use of fire.
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm, a common juristic phrase indicating permissibility or lack of prohibition.
key_terms.لَمْ تَمَسَّهُ النَّارُ: That fire has not touched it, referring to the method of drying or cooking.

ai.seo_question: Is dried meat that hasn't been cooked by fire permissible to eat according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates the consumption of *al-qadeed* (dried meat) preserved without fire, directly refuting the restrictive opinions of the companions of al-Mughira. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that preservation methods other than cooking, such as air-drying or salting, do not render the meat impure or impermissible, emphasizing ease in dietary laws.
